text: Matthew Dubourg (1703 – 3 July 1767) was an English violinist, conductor, and composer who spent most of his life in Ireland. He led the orchestra at the premiere of Georg Friedrich Handel's oratorio Messiah. Born in London as the illegitimate son of a court dancing master, with his mother's identity unknown, Dubourg performed a Corelli sonata at age nine in 1712 at the home of Thomas Britton, standing on a stool. At age eleven in 1714, he studied under the renowned Italian violinist, composer, and music theorist Francesco Geminiani and performed at the Queen's Theatre in March 1714, a benefit concert in May at Hickford's Room, and numerous other events during the London season. On 17 June 1727, he married Frances, daughter of musician Bernard Gates, at Stanmore, Middlesex; they had one daughter, Elizabeth, who married oboist Redmond Simpson on 22 September 1753, who had one child. Dubourg served as concert-master from 1728 to 1764 in Dublin, holding the official title "Chief Composer and Master of the Music attending His Majesty's State in Ireland" at Dublin Castle, and was a major force in Dublin's musical life alongside Geminiani, his long-time friend and teacher. In April 1730, Dubourg, styled "Mathew Dubourgh, Gentleman," entered into a property deal with Francis Barry, Senior, wife of Richard Barry of Dublin, whereby he received the dwelling house of tailor George Quay on Capel Street in Dublin for £110; the deed was witnessed by Elen Du Bourg (sic), possibly a relative. Four years later, a Deed of Mortgage or Conveyance was recorded between Frances Barry (widow of Richard Barry) and Dubourg, stating that Dubourg paid £460 for separate plots of land in Capel Street and Arbour Hill, Dublin; this deed was witnessed by Peter Gunan of Dublin, an instrument maker known for tuning and maintaining the organ at Trinity College Chapel. Dubourg was close friends with Handel and followed his career in London and the music scene across the Irish Sea. Around 15 May 1736, Benjamin Victor, theatre manager in London, wrote to Dubourg about the upcoming marriage of Frederick, Prince of Wales to Princess Augusta of Saxe-Gotha, noting that operas would not succeed due to the Prince's absence from public entertainments, and that music flourished in subscription concerts and private parties. Dubourg conducted the orchestra during the first performances of Handel's Messiah at Mr Neale's Music Hall in Dublin on 13 April 1742. Permission to use choir members from Dublin's cathedrals was initially granted by Dean Jonathan Swift (1667–1745), author of Gulliver's Travels, but Swift later withdrew it and reinstated it as the performance dates approached. Swift also criticized Dubourg's orchestra, calling them "a club of fiddlers in Fishamble Street," though Handel praised their performance, writing to Charles Jennens that the instruments were "really excellent" and the music "delightfully" sounded in the room. According to Redmond Simpson, Dubourg's son-in-law, Handel suffered a "violent and universal" paralytic stroke while dining with Dubourg in Dublin, but was quickly recovered by Doctors Barry and Quin and Mr Nichols, Surgeon General, through violent bleeding and evacuations, and never had a recurrence. During a 1742 concert conducted by Handel, Dubourg played a cadenza that wandered far from the theme, creating complex modulations, and when he returned to the original theme, Handel said, "Welcome home, Monsieur Dubourg." After the Messiah premiere, Dubourg traveled to London with Handel and performed several works at Covent Garden, including Samson, L'Allegro ed il Penseroso, and the London premiere of Messiah in 1743, before returning to Dublin in October. Dubourg composed several works still frequently performed, especially in Britain, including Variations of Druid Tunes, where he adapted famous Irish tunes in the late Baroque style, and variations on the sonatas (op. 5) of Arcangelo Corelli. In 1752, Dubourg became Master of the Royal Chapel in London, a position he held until his death in 1767. Upon Handel's death in 1759, money was left to Dubourg in his will. On 3 July 1767, Dubourg made a brief will leaving most of his estate to his wife Frances, and he died shortly thereafter; although there is some uncertainty about the exact date, his registered date of death is 5 July 1767. The inscription on his tombstone reads: "Here lyeth the body of Matthew Dubourg, chief composer and master of music in the kingdom of Ireland, servant to four generations of the illustrious House of Hanover, George I. and II., his Royal Highness the late Prince of Wales, and His present Majesty; as also instructor in Music to their Royal Highnesses the Duke of Cumberland and the late Prince Frederick. He died July 5, 1767, aged 64." Tho' sweet Orpheus thou couds't Bring Soft pleadings from the trembling string Unmov'd the King of Terror stands, Nor owns the magic of thy hands.
